resources.string: Holds messages for your contacts while they are offline, and delivers them when they come back. It cannot read them: they arrive already end-to-end encrypted and sealed a second time.
No address yet — Tor is still bootstrapping (30–60s on first run). An invite has no use without one.

One permanent code for everyone: scan it from Settings → Servers on a phone, or copy and paste it there. Unlimited people can join with the same code without asking you for anything — publish it once. Rotate it if it leaks; already-enrolled devices keep working.
No address yet — wait for Tor to finish starting
The current code stops working immediately. Anyone holding the old QR or link will not be able to join until you give them the new one. Devices that already enrolled are unaffected.
It will stop being able to deposit or fetch. Its messenger keeps working — it just falls back to peer-to-peer delivery.
This server always hosts an onion service. That is the only way a phone behind carrier NAT is reachable at all — no port forwarding, no domain, no certificate — so it is not something to switch off.
Also act as a relay and DHT node
Helps unrelated users find each other and connect. Independent of the mailbox: it carries live traffic blindly and stores nothing.
Not available on this device — set it manually in Settings → Battery.

Android can still kill a foreground service under memory pressure. This app is meant for a spare phone left plugged in; for a server that must never miss anything, run the typeon-server daemon on a small VPS.
Attachments are stored here. Identity and Tor state always stay in internal storage.
Unlike revoking, a blocked device cannot come back even with a fresh invite code. You can undo this later.
